extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers studying inductive logic and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for discovering causal laws by observation and experiment; guidance on analysing antecedents/consequents, composing causes, and when experiment vs observation is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Laws of Phenomena and Laws of Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish constant relations of succession or coexistence ('Laws of Phenomena') from laws that assign causes to effects ('Laws of Causation'); causes that human faculties can ascertain are themselves phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction is fundamental to framing a rigorous Canon of Induction. Avoid confusing mere regularities (succession/coexistence) with causal laws; using the word 'Cause' is legitimate and useful for expressing generality. Mistaken avoidance of the term risks obscuring important distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the joint effect of several causes is identical with the sum of their separate effects, the law of composition holds (example: mechanical transmission of motion/forces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle permits deductive prediction of combined effects from known separate effects and underlies why mechanics is a demonstrative science. It requires that the same law expressing the effect of each cause alone also correctly express the part due to that cause when combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of heteropathic combinations (when composition fails)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many domains (chemistry, organised bodies, life) combining causes produces phenomena heterogeneous to the separate causes; the joint effect is a new set of phenomena not reducible to a sum of separate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases are special and often require specific experiment; one cannot deduce compound behaviour simply from the properties of ingredients. Example: hydrogen + oxygen → water (new properties). Expect new laws to govern such combinations; treat them as distinct phenomena to be investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of mutual interference of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Either (a) concurrent causes each exert their full efficacy according to their separate laws (effects may algebraically add or subtract), or (b) concurrent causes alter one another and produce entirely different laws/phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which mode applies in a given case. In the first, apparent cancellation still fulfills each law (example: stream and drain); in the second, expect emergence of new laws (example: two liquids forming a solid). Use appropriate analytical methods for each mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of effects to causes is only a special case
rubrics_metrics.description: The common axiom that effects are proportional to their causes is a particular instance of composition (homogeneous causes) and fails where augmenting a cause changes the kind of effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious applying proportionality universally: when increasing a cause changes the qualitative outcome (e.g., heat causing expansion, then melting, then decomposition), proportional relations break down. Prefer the more comprehensive composition principle which subsumes proportional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the laws of causation in nature: determine the effects of every cause and the causes of every effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful induction would render the course of nature intelligible and predictable given requisite data. Frame investigations with this end—assign causes to effects and effects to causes through systematic inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental analysis (decomposition) as first step in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation is preceded by an analytic mental partition: decomposing complex antecedents/consequents into distinct elements to suggest what separations to effect in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental partition is indispensable but not sufficient; it guides which facts to seek and which experiments to perform. Poor mental analysis leads to missed details, conflation of observation with inference, vague quantities, or improper grouping. Cultivate the skill of discerning relevant components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for observing prepare the mind (no mechanical 'Art of Observing')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no strict art of observing; rules for observing are essentially instructions for preparing one's mind—self-education methods that make one capable of good observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on mental cultivation (attention, discrimination) rather than expecting a simple procedural checklist. Treat these rules as training habits that increase observational acuity rather than step-by-step laboratory technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying the circumstances (Baconian rule) is foundational
rubrics_metrics.description: To assign causes to effects we must vary circumstances so antecedents or consequents are found apart; this rule of varying the circumstances is the first and foundational rule of physical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire instances where specific antecedents occur without other potential antecedents, or consequents occur apart, to isolate causal relations. Use either natural instances (observation) or artificially arranged ones (experiment) to effect the necessary variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and experiment are logically equivalent but practically different
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no real logical distinction between observation and experiment; both vary circumstances and serve induction. Practically, experiment greatly extends observation by producing variations nature seldom supplies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method by practical considerations: use observation when nature provides appropriate separations; use experiment to create precise variations, increase the number of instances, or access conditions not available in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of experimentation: controllable, repeatable, and precise variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificially produced instances allow the investigator to place the phenomenon amid known circumstances and to decide what other conditions shall be present, facilitating clear inference about cause–effect relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can produce A artificially, control other simultaneous conditions to observe the effect of A. Experiments permit reproducibility, isolation of variables, and 'bringing the phenomenon home' for detailed study (example: electrical machine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity in observation: degree of minuteness depends on purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: How finely to decompose phenomena and how much to observe depends on the purpose: unnecessary detail (irrelevant circumstances) may be omitted, whereas essential distinctions must be pursued until they indicate needed observations/experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record what is materially relevant to your inquiry (e.g., planetary positions irrelevant to a typical chemical experiment). Carry mental decomposition only as far as required to identify experiments to be done, but remain ready to subdivide further if evidence demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to find antecedents or consequents apart for causal assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: If antecedents cannot be severed from one another or consequents never occur apart, a posteriori assignment of real laws is impossible; causal determination requires encountering separable instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observations/experiments to produce or locate cases where candidate antecedents occur without confounding accompaniments, or where consequents appear under differing prior conditions—this is essential for isolating true causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicting joint effects from separate agents requires invariance of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know effects of each cause acting separately, we can predict the joint effect deductively only if the same law that expresses each separate effect also correctly expresses the part due to that cause in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before summing separate effects, verify that laws remain unchanged in combination (mechanical forces are an example). When laws change upon combination (heteropathic case), deductive summation is invalid and empirical testing is required.
